g12-history-uh9-t1.overview: Indigenous knowledge is the knowledge and skills that a community builds outside formal schooling over centuries of experiment. This lesson defines it, sets out its thirteen unique features, and surveys the knowledge systems of Ethiopia's peoples.
objectives: Define indigenous knowledge and list its alternative names
Explain the thirteen unique characteristic features of indigenous knowledge
Describe how indigenous knowledge is transmitted and why much of it is being lost
Identify examples of Ethiopia's indigenous knowledge systems
Assess the need to document indigenous knowledge and preserve it for the future
g12-history-uh9-t1.simple: Indigenous knowledge, also called traditional or local knowledge, is the knowledge and practices that a community develops outside formal education over centuries of experiment in order to cope with its own environment. It covers skills, understandings and philosophies built through long interaction with nature, and it is part of the whole culture: language, healing, ritual and resource use. It passes from generation to generation mainly by word of mouth. Its features are that it is local, adaptive, cumulative, holistic, humble, intergenerational, invaluable, irreplaceable, moral, relative, responsible, spiritual and valid. Much of it is being lost because foreign technologies and modern education treat it as primitive, simple and static. Ethiopia is rich in such knowledge, in agriculture, architecture, medicine, cottage industry, philosophy and conflict resolution.
g12-history-uh9-t1.detailed:
Definition. Indigenous knowledge, also named traditional knowledge or local knowledge, is the knowledge systems and practices that people in each community have developed outside the formal educational system over centuries of experimentation, in an effort to cope with their own agro-ecological and socio-economic environments. It refers to the understandings, skills and philosophies developed by societies with long histories of interaction with their natural surroundings. It is also known as local knowledge, folk knowledge, people's knowledge, traditional wisdom or traditional science.

A cultural complex. Indigenous knowledge is integral to a cultural complex that encompasses all aspects of life: history, cultural practices, language, the environment and ecological relationships, resource use practices, social interactions, healing, ritual and spirituality. In short, it comprises knowledge systems and practices developed within a particular culture or society independently of, and prior to, the advent of the modern scientific knowledge system. That is why it is considered an important catalyst for sustainable overall development.

Transmission and loss. Indigenous knowledge passes from generation to generation, usually by word of mouth and cultural rituals, and through the wide range of other activities that sustain a society and its environment over many centuries. However, most of it disappears because of the intrusion of foreign technologies and development concepts that promise short-term gains or solutions without being able to sustain them. Colonial and western education also damaged the knowledge systems of African, Asian and Latin American countries, and even after independence modern education often treats indigenous knowledge as primitive, simple and static, so there is a grave risk that valuable knowledge about living sustainably is being lost.

Unique characteristic features. The textbook lists thirteen features. Indigenous knowledge is local, rooted in a particular place and unique to a given culture, since it is the lived experience of each community. It is adaptive, based on historical experiences yet changing with social, economic, environmental, spiritual and political conditions over millennia. It is cumulative, built from centuries of living in close proximity to nature through practical engagement, experience and trial and error. It is holistic, since all aspects of life are interconnected and are not considered in isolation but as parts of a whole. It is humble, teaching people not how to control nature but how to live in harmony with the gifts of the Creator. It is intergenerational, passed on as collective memory through language, stories, songs, ceremonies, legends and proverbs. It is invaluable, the key to sustainable social and economic development, and irreplaceable, since there is nothing western science can do to replace or replicate it.

Further features. Indigenous knowledge is also moral, holding that there is a right and a wrong way to interact with nature; relative, because it is not embodied to the same degree by all community members, and the elderly obviously carry more knowledge than younger members; responsible, since indigenous peoples generally believe they are responsible for the well-being of the natural environment around them; spiritual, rooted in a social context that sees the world in terms of social and spiritual relations among all life forms; and valid, since it does not require the validation of western science.

Ethiopia's knowledge systems. Ethiopia is an ancient country and the home of people with diverse cultures, so it is very rich in indigenous knowledge systems in areas such as agriculture, architecture, medicine, cottage industry, philosophy and conflict resolution. These systems are most often specific to a particular physical, economic and cultural environment, and they develop in response to production-associated problems such as land degradation, erosion, climate or weather change, changes in topography and changes in the economic, social and cultural settings of the community. Examples include the Obelisk of Aksum, the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, the castles of Gondar and the Wall of Harar in architecture; the local smelting of iron ores, tanning of hides and skins and weaving of clothes, which existed for centuries until the 20th century; the Oromo Gada system of indigenous democratic socio-political organization; the Afar Dagu information exchange system; Konso traditional skills in hillside terracing and banding; Dorze weaving skills; Surma traditional family planning methods; and Gumuz knowledge of shifting cultivation and natural resource management. In many rural parts of Ethiopia, a person struck by lightning is brought into contact with moist ground or dung, a practice that static electricity theory substantiates. Ethiopians are also rich in oral and written philosophical literature in Ge'ez, Arabic and other languages, in proverbs, songs and folktales, in well-developed traditional methods of conflict resolution and in knowledge of the medicinal properties of many plants.

keyTerms.def: The knowledge systems and practices that people in each community have developed outside the formal educational system over centuries of experimentation to cope with their own agro-ecological and socio-economic environments; also called traditional or local knowledge.
Another name for indigenous knowledge, passed from generation to generation usually by word of mouth and cultural rituals.
A feature of indigenous knowledge: collective memory is passed within a community from one generation to the next orally through language, stories, songs, ceremonies, legends and proverbs.
A feature of indigenous knowledge: all aspects of life are interconnected and are not considered in isolation but as parts of the whole.
The indigenous democratic socio-political system for which the Oromo people are renowned, practised long before the western idea of democracy reached Africa.
The indigenous and unique information exchange system of the Afar people, described in the textbook as the Internet of the Afar.
Small-scale home-based production such as smelting iron ores, tanning hides and skins and weaving clothes, long practised in rural Ethiopia and crucial to rural livelihoods.

workedExamples.problem: A rural community treats a person struck by lightning by bringing the survivor into contact with moist ground or dung. Is this mere superstition or valid knowledge?
workedExamples.given: The practice is used in many rural parts of Ethiopia; the survivor is placed in contact with moist ground or dung.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: indigenous knowledge is valid and does not require the validation of western science, yet it can often be explained by scientific principles.
workedExamples.substitution: Static electricity theory explains why moist ground or dung, which conduct electric charge, help a lightning-strike victim.
workedExamples.calculation: The practice does help the victim and has a scientific basis even though most rural people cannot explain it, so it satisfies the test of being valid knowledge.
workedExamples.answer: It is valid indigenous knowledge; the textbook notes that static electricity theory substantiates the practice.

workedExamples.problem: Why does an elderly villager often know more about local weather and planting than a young graduate trained in modern agriculture?
workedExamples.given: Indigenous knowledge is relative, and the elderly will obviously carry more knowledge than younger community members.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: indigenous knowledge is relative and cumulative, gained through long practical engagement with a particular local environment.
workedExamples.substitution: The elder has lived through far more seasons and trials in that specific place than the young graduate.
workedExamples.calculation: Because this knowledge grows with experience in a specific environment, the elder holds more of the local, cumulative knowledge that fits it.
workedExamples.answer: The elder carries more of the relative, cumulative local knowledge adapted to that environment.

workedExamples.problem: A community abandons its local seed selection after a foreign programme promises quick high yields. Using the features of indigenous knowledge, assess the risk.
workedExamples.given: Foreign technologies and development concepts promise short-term gains without being able to sustain them; indigenous knowledge is invaluable and irreplaceable.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: indigenous knowledge is cumulative, invaluable and irreplaceable, while imported solutions may not be able to sustain themselves.
workedExamples.substitution: Local seed knowledge built over centuries of trial and error cannot be replaced or replicated by western science, so dropping it destroys irreplaceable knowledge.
workedExamples.calculation: The short-term gain is weighed against a permanent loss of locally adapted knowledge, so the risk is high.
workedExamples.answer: High risk: abandoning indigenous knowledge can mean losing knowledge that nothing can replace.

workedExamples.problem: Why are many Ethiopian indigenous techniques described as area specific?
workedExamples.given: Ethiopian indigenous knowledge systems are most often specific to a particular physical, economic and cultural environment.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: indigenous knowledge is local, rooted in a particular place and generated by the people living there.
workedExamples.substitution: The techniques rely mainly on the local economic, social, cultural, religious and environmental situations.
workedExamples.calculation: Since each place has different conditions, the techniques that work there differ too, which makes them local, flexible and area specific.
workedExamples.answer: Because they are local responses to each community's own environment and conditions.

commonMistakes: Thinking indigenous knowledge is primitive, simple and static, the false view spread by colonial and western education.
Confusing indigenous knowledge with the knowledge taught in the formal school system.
Believing western science can fully replace or replicate indigenous knowledge.
Assuming all community members hold an equal amount of indigenous knowledge, ignoring that it is relative.
Treating the Gada system, the Dagu system or Konso terracing as mere custom rather than as working knowledge systems.
Believing an imported technology is always better simply because it promises quick results.
Ignoring the urgent need to document indigenous knowledge before it is lost.
applications: Recording proverbs, songs and folktales told by elders in your community before they are forgotten.
Asking a local farmer how he selects seed and when he plants, and comparing his reasons with the textbook.
Studying the Konso stone terraces as an example of soil conservation adapted to a dry highland environment.
Discussing how the Oromo Gada system practised democracy long before western democratic ideas reached Africa.
Interviewing an elderly person about traditional medicines and how plant knowledge was passed on.
Explaining in class why the lightning-strike practice can be justified by static electricity theory.
g12-history-uh9-t1.summary: Indigenous knowledge is the knowledge systems and practices that communities develop outside formal education over centuries of experimentation in order to cope with their own environments, and it passes from generation to generation mainly by word of mouth. Its thirteen features show that it is local, adaptive, cumulative, holistic, humble, intergenerational, invaluable, irreplaceable, moral, relative, responsible, spiritual and valid. Ethiopia is rich in such knowledge in agriculture, architecture, medicine, cottage industry, philosophy and conflict resolution, and it must be documented before it is lost.

g12-history-uh9-t2.overview: Heritage is the legacy of the past that a society keeps for present use and for future generations. This lesson explains the values and types of heritage and surveys the Ethiopian heritages registered by UNESCO.
objectives: Define heritage and distinguish cultural from natural heritage
Explain the values of heritage for identity, memory and nation building
Classify heritage as tangible or intangible with Ethiopian examples
Outline the categories and criteria used in registering world heritage
Describe Ethiopia's UNESCO-registered heritages and living traditions
g12-history-uh9-t2.simple: Heritage is the legacy of physical artifacts and intangible attributes that a group or society inherits from past generations, maintains in the present, and passes to future generations. It includes both the material and non-material culture of people as well as elements of nature. The World Heritage Convention of 1972 divides heritage into cultural and natural. Cultural heritage may be tangible, such as monuments and manuscripts, or intangible, such as festivals, music, drama and customs. Heritage gives people identity, collective memory and a sense of belonging, and it supports nation building. Ethiopia has nine World Heritage Sites, eight cultural and one natural, and UNESCO has also registered living traditions such as Meskel and Fiche Chambalala.
g12-history-uh9-t2.detailed:
What heritage is. Heritage is the legacy of physical artifacts and intangible attributes of a group or society that are inherited from past generations, maintained in the present, and bestowed for the benefit of future generations. In its broader sense it includes everything that people want to save, so heritage covers both the material and the non-material culture of man as well as elements of nature that man lives with. It comes to mean oral history or tradition, written history, buildings, landscapes, objects, pictures, memoirs, sounds and cultural beliefs.

Values of heritages. Heritage promotes the interpretation of the past by making relations with past people and events through shared experience. Its historical value mainly depends on direct experience of the elements that survived from the past, while its commemorative value lies in the meaning a heritage has for those who identify with it. Many heritage sites maintain a people's collective memory and identity, and war memorials or battlefields, public statues and palaces are memorials whose meanings are usually unforgettable. Heritage also serves as a symbol of nationalism and helps to define national identity, and it strengthens identities at the level of the home, neighbourhood, town and region as well as at continental and international level. It is an integral part of nation building and an instrument for creating a sense of belonging to a common place.

Types of heritage. According to the World Heritage Convention of 1972, heritage is broadly classified into two major categories, cultural and natural. Cultural heritage is any tangible or intangible object that is the product of the creativity and labour of man in pre-literary history and historical times, and it has scientific, historical, cultural, artistic and handcraft value. Tangible cultural heritage is that which can be seen and felt, and it is divided into movable and immovable historical and human-created heritage. Movable heritage is not attached to a foundation and can be moved easily from place to place; examples are parchment manuscripts, stone paintings and implements, and sculptures made of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone, as well as inscriptions of skin, ivory and horn. Heritage also includes natural reserves, museums, fauna, flora, geology, habitats and water, and landscapes such as national parks, gardens, coasts, mountain chains and natural areas.

Intangible heritage and Ge'ez literature. Intangible cultural heritage is that which cannot be touched and felt by the hands but can be seen or heard; it includes performances and shows, religious, wedding and mourning ceremonies, music, drama, literature and the cultural values, traditions and customs of the nation, nationalities and peoples. Much of Ethiopia's written heritage is in Ge'ez. Although Ge'ez literature is often said to be dominated by the Bible, there are many medieval and early modern original texts, most of them belonging to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, including Christian liturgy such as service books, prayers and hymns, and hagiographies; around 200 texts were written about indigenous Ethiopian saints from the 14th through the 19th centuries. Significant collections of Ethiopian manuscripts are found outside Ethiopia in France, Italy, the United Kingdom, Germany and the United States. The collection in the British Library comprises some 800 manuscripts dating from the 15th to the 20th centuries, initiated by a donation of 74 codices by the Church of England Missionary Society in the 1830s and 1840s and substantially expanded by 349 codices looted by the British from Meqdela, the last stronghold of Emperor Tewodros II, in the 1868 expedition to Ethiopia.

Mosques, palaces and walls. The Al Nejashi Mosque in the present-day Tigray region is the oldest Muslim religious place of worship found in northern Ethiopia. In the 7th century AD the first followers of the Prophet Mohammed were persecuted by the Quraysh ruling classes of Mecca, so in 615 A.D. the Prophet sent a small group, including his daughter and her husband Othman, to the Christian king of Aksum. The king, known as Ella Sham or Ashama b Abjar or Nejashi, refused the Meccan demand for their extradition, saying he would not hand over his guests even for a mountain of gold, and the Muslims stayed until they left back to Arabia in 628 A.D. In Jimma, King Abba Jifar II, the sixth ruler of a powerful Oromo-Muslim dynasty who reigned from 1877 to 1933, built a palace strongly influenced by Indian architecture, with the family mosque and reception room on the ground floor, the court room and private apartments on the first floor, and a watch tower whose windows open towards Shewa, Kafa, Wollega and the town of Jimma. The hereditary ruler of Wollega built Kumsa Moreda's Palace in the 1870s, and Sheikh Hojele al Hassan of Benishangul had a residence at Shegole in Addis Ababa, confiscated in 1975 under the proclamation that nationalized urban land and extra houses. The rulers of the medieval kingdom of Dawuro built defensive dry stone walls, locally called the Kati Halala Kella, and ditches between the 16th and 18th centuries, possibly against neighbouring enemies, Ahmed Gragn's war, the Oromo population expansion or pastoralist pressure; the walls counted three to seven rows, a single wall was estimated at 150 to 200 km, the seven rows totalled about 1,000 km, and the average height and width were about 2.6 m and 3.5 m.

UNESCO registered heritages of Ethiopia. Ethiopia currently has nine World Heritage Sites, of which eight are listed under the Cultural Heritage Criteria and only one, the Simen National Park, under the Natural Heritage Criteria. The Tiya Stone Erections in the Gurage Zone are 46 large decorated megaliths dated between the 10th and 15th centuries and were registered by UNESCO in 1980. The fortified historic town of Harar, about 526 km from Addis Ababa, has a 16th century wall called the Jegol with five traditional gates, and UNESCO regards the old town as the fourth city of Islam, with 82 mosques and 102 shrines; it was registered in August 2006. The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela and the castles of Gondar were registered in 1978 and 1979 respectively, the Konso Cultural Landscape is a 55-square-kilometre property of stone-walled terraces stretching back 21 generations, and the Simen National Park, established in 1969 and famous for the Gelada Baboon, Walia Ibex and Abyssinian Wolf, was registered in September 1978. Among living traditions, Meskel was registered by UNESCO as a World Heritage in September 2019, and Fiche Chambalala of the Sidama was registered in the same month.

Festivals and indigenous institutions. Ethiopia's intangible heritage is alive in its festivals. Ashenda, also called Ashendiye or Solel, is a colourful girls' festival among the Tigray, Agaw and Amhara peoples that commemorates the heavenly ascension of the Virgin Mary and is celebrated between 16 and 26 August. Timket, the Ethiopian Epiphany, commemorates the baptism of Jesus Christ in the River Jordan and begins on the eve of 18 January, called Ketera, with the main festival on 19 January. Meskel, on 26 September, commemorates the unearthing of the True Holy Cross and is celebrated with the Demera bonfire, and quarrels must be resolved before it, which makes it an occasion for reconciliation and peaceful coexistence. The Wolaita celebrate Gifaataa at the turn of their New Year, the Oromo celebrate Irreecha, the thanksgiving festival, at the beginning of Birraa at sacred lakes such as Hora Harsadi in Bishoftu, and the Sidama celebrate Fiche Chambalala, whose date is fixed each year by astrologers. Other indigenous institutions are the Oromo Gada system, an example of egalitarian democracy long before western democratic ideas reached Africa, the Sidama Luwa system, a generational class system whose five cycles of about eight years each make a full cycle of forty years, and the Afar Dagu information system.

keyTerms.def: The legacy of physical artifacts and intangible attributes of a group or society that are inherited from past generations, maintained in the present and bestowed for the benefit of future generations.

Any tangible or intangible object that is the product of the creativity and labour of man in pre-literary history and historical times, with scientific, historical, cultural, artistic and handcraft value.
Cultural heritage that can be seen and felt, further divided into movable and immovable historical and human-created heritage.
Heritage that cannot be touched and felt by the hands but can be seen or heard, such as ceremonies, music, drama, literature, traditions and customs.
Heritage not attached to a foundation that can be moved from place to place easily, such as parchment manuscripts, sculptures and inscriptions.
Elements of nature that people live with, such as natural reserves, fauna, flora, geology, habitats, water and landscapes.
The international agreement according to which heritage is broadly classified into the two major categories of cultural and natural.
The 16th century wall surrounding the old town of Harar, with five traditional gates, still intact and the symbol of the town and its inhabitants.

workedExamples.problem: Is everything that is old a heritage? Justify your answer using the definition of heritage.
workedExamples.given: Heritage is the legacy of physical artifacts and intangible attributes that a group inherits from the past, maintains in the present and passes on; in its broader sense it is everything people want to save.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: heritage is defined by inheritance, present maintenance and value for future generations, not by age alone.
workedExamples.substitution: An old object that no one preserves and that carries no meaning or value for a group is neither maintained nor bestowed.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the object fails the tests of collective value and transmission to the future, age alone does not make it heritage.
workedExamples.answer: No. Age alone does not make something heritage; it must be valued, kept and passed on.

workedExamples.problem: Why was the first mosque in Ethiopia established in the present-day Tigray region?
workedExamples.given: In 615 A.D. the Prophet Mohammed sent persecuted followers to the Christian king of Aksum; the king refused to hand them back and granted them protection until 628 A.D.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: heritage sites often record moments of refuge, tolerance and contact between communities.
workedExamples.substitution: Aksum was a Christian kingdom known for justice and truth, so it was chosen as a safe place, and the followers were allowed to practise their religion freely.
workedExamples.calculation: The first Muslims found protection there, so the mosque later built in that place marks the event and its meaning.
workedExamples.answer: Because the Aksumite king sheltered the first Muslims in 615 A.D., and the Al Nejashi Mosque was built there to remember it.

workedExamples.problem: A heritage site in your locality is neglected and partly destroyed. Using the values of heritage, argue why it should be conserved.
workedExamples.given: Heritage maintains collective memory and identity, promotes interpretation of the past, serves nation building and creates a sense of belonging.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: the values of heritage are historical, commemorative, identity-building and socio-political.
workedExamples.substitution: Losing the site would remove direct experience of the past and weaken local identity and belonging.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the site carries several heritage values at once, its loss harms both collective memory and community cohesion.
workedExamples.answer: Conserve it: it carries historical, commemorative and identity values for present and future generations.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia has nine World Heritage Sites, yet many more sites meet UNESCO criteria. What does this gap mean for heritage policy?
workedExamples.given: The number of registered Ethiopian sites is apparently too small compared with the numerous cultural and religious heritage materials and sites.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: registration depends on meeting the criteria of the World Heritage Convention of 1972 through documentation, nomination and priority.
workedExamples.substitution: If many sites qualify but are not registered, the problem lies in documentation and nomination rather than in the heritage itself.
workedExamples.calculation: The gap shows an unrealized registration potential, so the textbook calls registration a priority agenda for all concerned bodies.
workedExamples.answer: It means registration should be a priority, since many qualifying Ethiopian heritages remain unregistered.

commonMistakes: Believing that anything old is automatically a heritage.
Thinking heritage is only monuments and buildings, and forgetting intangible heritage such as festivals, music and customs.
Treating natural heritage as less important than cultural heritage, although Ethiopia has only one natural site registered.
Assuming registration by UNESCO ends the duty to preserve a site; heritages must be preserved even after designation.
Confusing movable heritage, such as manuscripts, with immovable heritage, such as walls and castles.
Forgetting that Ge'ez literature includes works of history, ecclesiastical and civil law, philology and medicine, not only religious texts.
Treating all Ethiopian festivals as one and the same, instead of noticing that Ashenda, Timket, Meskel, Gifaataa, Irreecha and Fiche Chambalala belong to different peoples.
applications: Visiting a local church, mosque or old building and listing what makes it heritage for the community.
Collecting the names and registration dates of Ethiopia's World Heritage Sites and the criteria under which each is listed.
Interviewing elders about a festival in your area and recording its meaning and rituals.
Explaining why Meskel promotes reconciliation, since personal quarrels and social disagreements must be resolved before the celebration.
Discussing why the Ge'ez manuscripts looted from Meqdela and now held abroad matter for Ethiopian heritage.
Writing a short case for why the Bale Mountains National Park should be registered by UNESCO.
g12-history-uh9-t2.summary: Heritage is the legacy of physical artifacts and intangible attributes inherited from past generations, maintained in the present and passed to the future, and the World Heritage Convention of 1972 classifies it into cultural and natural types. Cultural heritage may be tangible, such as the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela and the Jegol of Harar, or intangible, such as Meskel, Timket and the Gada system. Heritage gives identity, collective memory and belonging, which is why registering and conserving Ethiopia's sites and living traditions is a priority.

questions.q: The Sidama Luwa system passes through five generational cycles; one full cycle is:
